extracted.intended_audience: prospective bush traders, coastal/black middlemen, and colonial store agents operating in West African interior trade
extracted.subtask_description: Practical norms and survival/business practices for running a bush factory and trading with interior tribes (Fans, Igalwa, etc.) on the West African coast. Includes security, store layout, local-credit and marriage-alliance tactics, pricing and customer-management advice drawn from first-hand experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factory layout and secure storage
rubrics_metrics.description: The factory should be built on poles above the ground with the space under the house used as a store for rubber in barrels and ebony in billets; piles of billets and goods should be placed in a clean, sandy yard and surrounded by a stout stockade, main face to the river.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Agonjo factory was 'mounted on poles above the ground; the space under the house being used as a store for rubber...'; keeping goods elevated and within sight from the verandah lets the trader 'hover over these precious possessions' day and night. Stockade placement and river frontage considerations are important for access and defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constant personal vigilance over stock
rubrics_metrics.description: The trader must remain close to his goods—sleeping and waking near them—to guard against theft, damage, and raids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author metaphor: 'hover over these precious possessions, sleeping and waking, like a sitting hen over her eggs.' Practical implication: keep stores accessible to the trader, position living quarters to command the yard, and maintain nightly watch.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'No admittance except on business' policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Strictly enforce entry rules: admit only genuine business customers to avoid permanent occupation of premises and loss of control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: permitting customers to invade premises leads to them 'making themselves at home' and renders the house no longer the trader's. Enforce evictions and deny non-business access to preserve authority and security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt a firm, authoritative persona ('Devil man')
rubrics_metrics.description: The trader must 'betray no weakness' and present an uncompromising character—combining shrewdness, firmness, political tact, and language skills—to command respect and deter theft or coercion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author describes this composite persona as 'a compound of the best parts of Cardinal Richelieu, Brutus, Julius Caesar, Prince Metternich, and Mezzofanti' to emphasize diplomacy, firmness, and multilingual ability. Firmness converts aggressive behavior into respectful daytime trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent customers from camping on premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not tolerate customers sleeping all over the premises or intruding into kitchens and dining areas; otherwise the trader loses control of his house and stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include nuisance, theft, and permanent loss of exclusive use. Maintain separation between private/store spaces and customer access; evict or restrict late-night occupiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain predictable trade routes and schedules
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow definite trade routes and expected visiting schedules (e.g., twice a year) so villages know when to expect you and won't panic or retaliate if you are absent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularity provides trader safety because neighboring villages police one another by reputation: if a trader disappears from the route, villages investigate and may punish the offending village. Missing expected visits undermines trust and disrupts commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use marriage alliances to secure local protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate wives across villages along the trade route to secure cooking, trustworthy local advocates, and protection from local reprisals or theft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wives act as devoted caretakers of a trader's food (preventing poisoning), create kin ties that integrate the trader into maternal kin networks, and provide local influence—one trader's wives could 'stretch over 300 miles of country.' This is presented as the primary local security mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and accommodate local commission/customary distribution (nyeno)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that chiefs and principal men will take an understood commission (nyeno) from opened goods and that goods will be divided and traded in stages through middlemen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trader should factor nyeno and the resulting distribution chains into pricing and stock planning; understand that goods often leave villages on trust and that the trader will therefore carry outstanding debts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage credit and expect outstanding debts
rubrics_metrics.description: Be prepared to extend goods on trust to chiefs or principal men, resulting in a quantity of debts outstanding in each village liable to be bad debts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: keep careful accounts, limit exposure where possible, and know that trust-credit is an endemic feature of bush trade; devise ways (local alliances, nyeno arrangements) to mitigate losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide adequate rations and decent housing for staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Firms should take care of their employees (beach hands, kruboys) with ample, good rations and good houses; well-kept factories retain staff and function better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative note: firms that neglected staff led to poor living conditions and higher mortality among white agents; better provisioned factories (e.g., Hatton and Cookson) were more successful. Good staff provisioning supports logistics and security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid raising prices abruptly; manage pricing credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not raise prices to cover short-term issues because 'Africans can understand prices going up, but never prices coming down'—raising prices risks losing trade permanently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prices are perceived as arbitrary or increasing, buyers will withhold trade until price falls (which may never happen), potentially ruining the district's commerce. Maintain stable, credible pricing strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist being bullied into paying fancy prices or giving away goods
rubrics_metrics.description: When first opening trade in a district, customers may try to frighten the trader into paying high prices or accepting useless goods; the trader must resist such pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early-stage traders are vulnerable to intimidation and inflated local demands; success requires not giving way to threats and preserving firmness to secure fair trade terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice travel and weather-aware vigilance
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise heightened caution when traveling or trading at night, in inky blackness, or during violent weather (tornado nights); these conditions increase risk of raids or accidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moonlight nights are relatively safer; when dark or stormy the trader must be 'very much out and about' and vigilant. Plan travel and guarding accordingly to minimize exposure during high-risk conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand local currencies, valuations, and marriage-price systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Know local forms of coinage and high-value cultural exchanges (e.g., Fans use bikei—little iron imitation axe-heads bundled as ntet—for the price of a wife) to operate effectively in the economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical trading requires cultural literacy: the trader should recognize how goods, iron tokens, and local prestige translate into economic and social claims (marriage, status), and price goods accordingly.
